pr.title: The transport arrives: field plays live on Windows over a named pipe (windows-portability.md chunks 4-5)
pr.head: beb3394e67b617919f4dfad00e2a65131bb8f401

summary: field-audiod is the native audio daemon. The CLI spawns it on demand for each project and talks to it over a control channel that carries newline-delimited JSON requests and broadcast events. The daemon exits on its own when idle. On macOS and Linux that channel is a Unix domain socket at .field/audiod.sock. Node cannot open a Unix socket on Windows, and the daemon's socket code was POSIX-only, so until this change field play, field transport and live rendering could not run on Windows at all.

This pull request gives Windows its own transport: a named pipe, the Windows local IPC object that Node dials natively. The CLI derives the pipe's name from the project root and hands it to the daemon with --socket, so both ends use one string. The pipe admits only the user who runs the daemon, and only from the local machine. In the daemon, request handling moves above the I/O layer and is shared by both platforms. Only accepting, reading, writing and shutting down split per platform, and the POSIX arm moves unchanged.

Two small pieces of the same plan ride along. field play without a built daemon now refuses the afplay fallback on every platform except macOS, before it announces the fallback. CI also gains a windows-latest job. The tests that were skipped on Windows until the transport existed run there now, the recording tests included, with two exceptions the plan tracks: crash recovery fails on the Windows runner for a reason not yet found, and the MIDI take tests have no source to record, because Windows has no virtual MIDI ports for field keys to publish. The Python generation workers keep their POSIX transport, which is a later chunk of the plan.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Named pipe: Windows local IPC, addressed as \\.\pipe\name. A server creates instances, and each client connection uses one instance.
  • Parked instance: the one instance the daemon keeps ready for the next client.
  • ConnectNamedPipe: the server call that waits for a client on an instance. With overlapped (asynchronous) I/O it returns at once and completes later through an OVERLAPPED record and an event.
  • FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE: makes instance creation fail if the name already exists, which gives the one-owner guarantee.
  • DACL: the access list on a Windows object, saying which accounts may open it and how.
  • CancelIoEx: cancels the I/O pending on a handle at that moment. Later I/O is unaffected.
  • SHUT_RD: the POSIX half-close the socket arm uses. Every later read returns end-of-file.
  • Idle exit: the daemon quits when no client is connected, nothing plays, and it has been quiet for the idle period.
  • MessageManagerLock: JUCE's lock on the daemon's message thread. Every request but session takes it.

cards.title: Review history so far
cards.html:
• The author's own reviews on a63ec97 found an OVERLAPPED record the kernel could write after its stack frame was gone, on the ordinary shutdown path. It is fixed: every accept iteration now reaps a pending connect before it exits.
  • The afplay guard widened from Windows to every non-macOS platform after #162's review, and the plan's §2.2 records why.
  • Projector's review on 1eff8a0 found that field play announced the afplay fallback before refusing it.
  • Projector's review on 6a529d1 found an accept-loop spin, a pipe readable by every local account, docs/architecture.md left behind, and wrong CI comments.
  • All five are fixed at 7355d7d, along with the shutdown read gap that review listed as a suggestion. Projector's review there was clean.
  • 0b26d94 merges the base and fixes or skips the tests that failed on the first windows CI run. Projector's review there was clean, and both CI jobs then passed on it, windows included.
  • beb3394 merges main's keyboard and MIDI work in through the base, and lifts record-midi-daemon's guard. Main's MIDI requests ride the shared request handling, so the pipe serves them. Projector's review there is clean, and a human approval is what remains. Every Projector review read the code without running it, because the pull request's author has no write access to the repository.

groups.title: The pipe name both ends agree on
groups.kicker: How the CLI names a project's pipe and tells the daemon
intro: Every command that reaches the daemon asks socketPathFor where it is. On POSIX the answer stays a path relative to the current directory, which keeps it inside the 104-byte limit on socket paths. On Windows the function now returns a pipe name instead: field- followed by 24 hex characters of a SHA-256 over the resolved project root, lowercased, and the socket's relative path. Lowercasing matters because NTFS compares paths without regard to case, and two spellings of one root must reach one daemon.
When the CLI has to spawn the daemon, it passes the same string with --socket. POSIX keeps passing the relative path, which the daemon binds against its working directory, the project root.

checks.text: Every caller of socketPathFor hands the result to net.connect or server.listen, except helloIfRunning in src/commands/version.ts, which first calls existsSync on it. That file is not in this diff. On Windows the check stats a pipe name, and Node's existsSync stats by opening the path, so field --version opens and closes the pipe. The daemon's accept loop handles that client; see the next group.

files.note: The Windows branch of socketPathFor: a hashed pipe name per project root and socket.

checks.text: Lowercasing covers case only. An 8.3 short name, a subst drive or a junction is another spelling of the same root and hashes to a different pipe. The review lists hashing realpathSync.native(root) as a suggestion.

files.note: The spawn passes the full pipe name on Windows and the relative socket path elsewhere.

checks.text: path here is the same value tryConnect dials, so on Windows the daemon binds exactly the name the client opens.

groups.title: The daemon's Windows transport
groups.kicker: Shared request handling above, a named-pipe accept, read and shutdown loop below
intro: server.cpp now has one copy of request handling for both platforms: handleLine parses a line, dispatch runs the operation, and broadcast sends an event to every open connection. Below that, an #if defined(_WIN32) arm implements the destructor, start, acceptLoop, readLoop, send, beginShutdown and sweepClosedConnections with Win32 handles. The #else arm is the POSIX code, moved as it was.

Every pipe instance gets the same security descriptor from pipeSecurity(): a protected DACL that grants access to the user running the daemon and to nobody else, which is what the POSIX socket's file permissions give. Every instance also rejects clients on other machines. Without these, Windows' default descriptor would let every local account read the pipe.

start creates the first pipe instance with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE, so a second daemon for the same project fails there. acceptLoop then runs one overlapped ConnectNamedPipe at a time on the parked instance. It polls every 200 ms rather than waiting forever, because the shutdown wake-up can be lost. When a client arrives, the loop parks a fresh instance, hands the connected one to a new reader thread, and goes round again. When no client arrives, it disconnects the instance before trying again.

The POSIX arm half-closes each socket with SHUT_RD, so readers see end-of-file and the drain loop in main.cpp can finish. Windows has no such state. beginShutdown uses CancelIoEx to cancel each pending read, and readLoop checks running both before and after it issues each read, so no read outlives shutdown. After the loop, a reader drains exactly the bytes buffered at that moment, which matches what SHUT_RD still delivers.

checks.text: The POSIX arm and the shared request handling match the base. The review extracted both halves from the base and the head at 6a529d1 and diffed them, and every later commit to server.cpp touches only the Windows arm. The only differences are blank lines and the processId() helper that replaces ::getpid() in hello.

No Windows code here was compiled or run during the review, because the head is untrusted. CI was read instead. On 0b26d94 the windows job compiled this file under MSVC, access and accept-loop fixes included, and the whole suite passed over the pipe. The jobs on beb3394 were still running when this summary was written.

Main's change to this file, the record-midi feature and arm's kind: "midi", landed in the shared dispatch above the platform split, so the Windows arm serves it. The review read where the merge placed it.

files.note: Shared request handling, then the Windows arm (security, accept, read, write, shutdown on pipe handles), then the POSIX arm unchanged.

checks.text: The descriptor is a protected DACL, D:P(A;;GA;;;<user SID>), built once from the process token. start() refuses when it cannot be built rather than falling back to the default descriptor, which grants read to Everyone. Generic-all for the user includes FILE_CREATE_PIPE_INSTANCE, so the daemon can still create later instances. Checked by reading against Microsoft's CreateNamedPipe documentation.
PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS is set on both CreateNamedPipeA calls through this one constant. Each instance chooses its own remote-client mode, so both calls need it.
The bounded poll. A SetEvent from beginShutdown can land before the ResetEvent at the top of the iteration and be lost, so the loop re-reads running every 200 ms.

Every exit from an accept iteration with a connect still pending passes this block. The block cancels the connect and waits for the kernel to finish with ov before the stack frame ends. The review traced the break, the continue and the accept path.

A client that opens the parked instance and closes it before ConnectNamedPipe leaves the call failing with ERROR_NO_DATA until the server disconnects the instance. This call does that, so the next ConnectNamedPipe pends as usual. On the other paths into this branch the instance has no client, and the call fails without effect. Checked against Microsoft's ConnectNamedPipe documentation.

beginShutdown clears running before it calls CancelIoEx, and this check runs after ReadFile is issued. Either the shutdown's cancel finds the read, or this check sees the flag and cancels the read through its own OVERLAPPED.
The shutdown drain peeks once and reads exactly that many bytes, because peeking again would follow a client that keeps writing.
A null OVERLAPPED cancels every I/O on the handle, so a write still waiting on a full pipe buffer is cancelled too. The comment says so.

files.note: Connection and Server state split per platform: a pipe handle, the parked instance and the accept event on Windows; the descriptors and the lock on POSIX.

groups.title: No afplay fallback off macOS
groups.kicker: field play without a built daemon refuses on Windows and Linux
intro: Without a built daemon, field play on macOS falls back to playing artifacts through afplay, a macOS command. On any other platform that spawn could only fail with an error that names a tool the machine never had. The field play action now throws the build hint first, before it prints that it is using afplay. Plan §2.2 decides there is no Windows fallback, and its amendment widens that to every platform but macOS.

files.note: The platform check opens the !daemonBinary() branch, and playWithAfplay's comment says the caller refuses.

checks.text: Off macOS the only output is the build hint: this check runs before the refusal for --from and the other daemon-only flags, and before the "using afplay" line. playWithAfplay has no other caller.

groups.title: Tests that run on Windows now
groups.kicker: Retired skip guards, platform-neutral assertions, and a cleanup that waits for the daemon
intro: Until the transport existed, every test that dialed the daemon or faked one was skipped on Windows. Those guards come off here. That covers the protocol, play-daemon and live-session suites, the live plugin-hosting chains, the click, punch and record tests, and the nine fake-daemon tests in version.test.ts, whose fakes now listen on whatever socketPathFor returns.

One Windows behaviour needed a helper. Windows cannot delete a directory that is a live process's working directory, and the daemon takes a few hundred milliseconds to exit after quit. removeTempProject in src/testing/temp.ts retries the whole removal for up to ten seconds, and returns on its first try on POSIX. The credentials test skips its POSIX mode-bit asserts on Windows, which reports no mode bits.

The first windows CI run, on 6a529d1, failed in four groups, and this head answers each. The hosted-chain tests could not find their plugin, which the base's FIELD_PLUGIN_PATH fix answers. The clone, push and pull tests passed file://C:\… to git-lfs, which could not parse it, so they now build the URL with pathToFileURL. The inventory-cache test rewrote a file inside one change-time tick, so it now waits one out on Windows. The crash-recovery test lost its connection for a reason not yet found, so it skips on Windows, and plan §7.2 tracks it.

Main's MIDI take tests come in through the base, guarded on Windows as serve-mode tests. This pull request lifts that guard. The tests that advertise record-midi, and that refuse to arm with no source, run over the pipe. The take tests skip on Windows, because they need field-audiod --keys to publish a virtual MIDI source and Windows has no virtual MIDI ports.

checks.text: Each test file that drops an rmSync call still uses rmSync elsewhere or no longer imports it. The repository's tsconfig.json sets noUnusedLocals, so a stale import would fail pnpm typecheck. Checked by grep at this head.

files.note: New helper: retries a recursive delete for up to ten seconds while a daemon exits.

checks.text: The fake daemon is a Node pipe server on Windows. Node keeps several instances listening, unlike the real daemon's one parked instance, so these tests cannot exercise the accept-loop behaviour in server.cpp.

This test decides the killed daemon is gone from process.kill(pid, 0). The review offers one lead, inferred and not verified: on Windows that check can succeed before the dying process has closed its handles, so the fresh connect could reach the old daemon's pipe instance and see it close. Plan §7.2 names a different candidate in the capture code.

Windows only. A --keys refusal there counts as no source available, the way a Linux machine without the ALSA sequencer already does, and the take test skips. A helper that cannot publish anywhere else still fails the test.
Windows only. The cache keys on size, mtime and ctime, and NTFS stamps ctime from a clock that advances in ticks of about 15.6 ms. The comment marks that cause as inferred.

pathToFileURL(bare).href is file:///tmp/… on macOS and Linux, the same URL the old file://${bare} gave, and file:///C:/… on Windows, which git-lfs parses. The push and pull tests make the same change.

groups.title: CI, the architecture doc, and the plan's record
groups.kicker: A windows-latest job, docs/architecture.md on the pipe, and windows-portability.md marking chunks 4 and 5 implemented
intro: The new windows job runs what the Linux job runs, except the Python type checks, because the workers stay on their POSIX transport. The workflow's header now describes both jobs and what the Windows job costs: twice the Linux per-minute rate, and a cold JUCE build whenever the cache is evicted.

docs/architecture.md describes the system as it is, so it now says that on Windows the daemon listens on a named pipe, that FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE keeps it to one per project, and that the pipe admits only its user.

The plan records chunk 4 and chunk 5 as implemented, amends §2.2 to cover every platform but macOS, and answers two of its §6 open questions. A third is mostly answered: one manual test, a physical unplug during playback, stays open. The plan stays at in-progress.

files.note: Adds the windows job, and rewrites the header to cover both jobs.

checks.text: The paragraph after this one still opens "What that gives up", meaning the dropped macOS job, but it now follows this Windows-cost paragraph. The review lists moving one of them as a suggestion.
This key is the Linux job's key character for character, and it already varies by runner.os, so the two jobs never share a cache. Checked against line 79.

files.note: The daemon section and the IPC section now cover the Windows named pipe.

checks.text: The IPC passage also says the workers keep their Unix sockets, so they do not run on Windows. That matches plan §4.
